name: PT Golden Energy Mines Tbk

frontmatter.title: Golden Energy Mines — a low-cost contract-of-work thermal producer whose dividend, not the price, carries the value
frontmatter.summary: GEMS is a low-cost contractor-operated Indonesian thermal coal miner inside the DSSA/Sinar Mas group. We refresh at HOLD: with the royalty charged at the rate the LK shows being paid and the peak-dividend cross-check excluded, our finite-life through-cycle DCF sits just below the market price, so the dividend, not a re-rating, carries the return; the swing factors are the realised-price discount and the through-cycle marker.
thesis: Through-cycle value, not spot earnings, anchors the call: our finite-life reserve DCF, priced off the house coal deck long-run Newcastle marker and the FY2025A realised ratio, now sits at about the market price — so the expected return is carried by the dividend rather than by a re-rating.

The royalty is charged the way the LK shows it being paid: GEMS mines under contract-of-work licences whose share-of-production royalty the contract states, so we charge that contract rate flat — not the IUPK succession schedule for ex-contract holders, which is a licence class GEMS does not hold.

The realised-price discount is the largest single swing both ways: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the FY2025A actual and hold it flat, and it is the discount, not the marker, that a low-CV, domestic-heavy producer is really exposed to.

The reserve base is finite and disclosed: at the sales pace the stated reserves are consumed inside the model horizon, so the DCF has no perpetuity tail — and it carries no explicit mine-closure charge, which we disclose rather than shock.

The dividend is the market anchor, but we do not bank it: the group pays out most of its parent profit, so the yield is high — and the cross-check that capitalised that yield is excluded from the target because it prices a peak-year payout, so the question the model poses is whether the through-cycle price funds the payout every year.
Governance is concentrated: an ultra-low free float inside a family-controlled group means minority holders own the economics but not the decisions.

catalysts.event: FY2026 interim dividend paid to shareholders
FY2026 production-and-sales outcome against the company target
FY2026 audited financial statements and final dividend proposal

blocks.text: We refresh coverage of PT Golden Energy Mines at **HOLD** with a target of **Rp6,607**, a total return of **6.6%** against the last price of Rp7,450. The call rests on our primary method — a finite-life, through-cycle discounted cash flow of the reserve base — which values the company at Rp8,153, close to the market. Our EV/EBITDA cross-check sits alongside it at Rp7,382, and our target blends the two (weights 71% and 29%); the dividend-yield cross-check, which screens far above both, is **excluded** because it capitalises the FY2026E peak payout — and excluding it is what takes the call from ADD to HOLD. With the price near the resource value, the expected return is carried by the dividend rather than by a re-rating [S0].

GEMS is a low-cost, contractor-operated thermal coal miner in the DSSA / Sinar Mas group, selling a low-calorific Indonesian product into a domestic-heavy book with Chinese and Indian export offtake [S3]. Coal sales of 54.9 Mt (F1) generated revenue of US$2,414.1m in FY2025 (F10) at a realised price of 40.5% of the Newcastle marker. The company targets up to 58.0 Mt of production and sales in 2026 [S6].

Three things move the value. First, the **realised price**: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the FY2025A actual and hold it flat at 40.5%, so the DCF does not inherit the FY2026E benchmark spike of 137.0 USD/t — a ratio fitted to a spike would carry a trough relationship into the long run. The discount reflects the low-CV product and the large domestic offtake; the bull case reverts the ratio part-way toward its through-cycle level while the bear carries the trough-year discount as the new normal — the same driver, mirrored. Second, the **royalty**: GEMS mines under contract-of-work licences, whose share-of-production royalty the LK states as 13.5% of coal produced (F9), and the LK's own royalty line sits in the same band across three audited years (US$312.4m in FY2025, F7); we charge that contract rate flat at 12.9% of revenue, because the IUPK succession schedule is a licence class GEMS does not hold — the earlier read charged that band by assertion, which overstated cost and understated value, and this refresh corrects it [S3]. Third, the **reserve life**: the disclosed 844.4 Mt (F3) are consumed inside the horizon at the modelled sales rate, so this is a finite-life value with no terminal tail — and no mine-closure charge, which we disclose rather than shock.

Coal miners in Indonesia are usually valued on the worth of the tonnes in the ground at a normalised
price, not on one year's earnings, because earnings swing with the seaborne price while the resource
does not. A low-cost producer keeps a margin through a trough that a high-cost producer loses, so
cost position — not the spot price — is what separates a survivor from a name that needs a
permanently high price to justify its value.

GEMS mines and trades thermal coal through a set of Indonesian subsidiaries. It reports two segments — coal mining and coal trading — plus a small "others" leg, and coal mining is effectively the whole business: the trading segment's revenue and cost of revenue near-offset, leaving the mining leg to carry group profit [S3]. Export sales run mainly to China and India, while domestic sales are the majority of revenue measured at the port of sale, with China the largest single destination country and Indonesia close behind [S3]; the group is looking to add destinations beyond its core China-India book [S6], which matters because the export leg carries the price upside while the domestic leg is capped, so mix between the two moves realised price without moving volume.

The product is a lower-calorific Indonesian thermal coal: the realised price in FY2025 stood at 40.5% of the Newcastle marker, a discount that reflects both quality and the large domestic offtake [S0, S3]. The company has not disclosed a strip ratio, so our intensity factor is an assumption tied to the group's wider coal book, but the cost reality is visible in the margin: the contractor-operated model runs a small capital-expenditure line (US$19.2m, F11) and a working-capital cycle dominated by receivables and payables rather than inventory [S0, S3].

The group is acquisitive — several licence holders in the reserve statement entered through business combinations — and goodwill is tested annually for impairment, with charges taken on weaker cash-generating units in recent years [S3]. It runs a portfolio of concessions across Kalimantan and Sumatra through subsidiary licence holders, and the reserve statement lists the blocks individually and reconciles them to one group total (F3, F4), which tells us the assets are managed as one book rather than as discrete mines [S3]. The strategy is volume-led and cost-led rather than price-led: because the product is a commodity, the management lever is tonnes and cost per tonne, and the group buys scale through adjacent licences and a trading leg that moves third-party coal alongside its own [S3]. GEMS is a subsidiary of PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA), inside the Sinar Mas group, and is the vehicle through which the bulk of the group's listed coal volume flows; the free float is a small fraction of the shares [S0].

Seaborne thermal-coal demand is driven by Chinese and Indian power generation, and Indonesia is the largest exporter. An Indonesian producer's realised price does not track the Newcastle benchmark directly: the discount at which its lower-grade coal clears, and the regulated price for domestic power-station tonnes, create a wide and persistent gap between marker and received price. Our sector deck prices this name against the reviewed Newcastle benchmark series; the Indonesian index series are not useable as pricing inputs, so the whole product discount is carried in our realisation assumption rather than in a national index [S3].

Regulation defines the economics. Royalties sit inside cost of revenue: the group's contract-of-work licences carry a fixed share-of-production royalty (F9), and because a coal contract of work keeps its own PNBP terms until the contract term ends, GEMS's royalty does not step with the government reference price the way the newer IUPK succession schedule does — a licence class GEMS does not hold, so the state's take here is a stable share of the selling price rather than a rising band [S3]. The domestic market obligation caps the price on domestic power tonnes, which mutes the domestic leg's upside in a strong market, and mine licences are finite but extendable with reserve consumption reconciled each year (F3, F4) [S3]. We carry the domestic-market-obligation link as an inert input: the power-cap model is set to the domestic power cap of 70.0 USD/t against a realised price below it, so it binds nothing at today's prices and does not move value; the share of volume assumed under the cap is an engine-default proxy with no disclosed power-versus-industrial tonnage split behind it, so it is held as insurance only and the DMO's bite is tested through the bear volume shock, not through the cap [S3].

Competitively, GEMS is a large-volume, low-cost producer: our LK-calibrated cash cost sits at the low end of the Indonesian cost curve on the tonnes the LK discloses, which leaves a margin through the trough; we call it calibrated low cost rather than a first-quartile rank, which would need a named cost-curve source we do not have [S3]. Its edge is that cost position plus the group's integrated marketing and logistics reach, not a differentiated product. Buyer power is material (large Chinese and Indian utilities, a regulated domestic buyer); supplier power is low (competing mining contractors); substitution from renewables and gas is a slow structural threat; new entry is gated by RKAB permitting; and rivalry is intense on price but disciplined on volume when the quota bites.

Industry size and growth. The seaborne thermal market is enormous but its growth is now a zero-sum game between exporting nations: Indonesian supply, gated by the annual RKAB quota, competes with Australian, Russian and South African tonnes for Chinese and Indian demand that is itself slowing as domestic mining restarts and energy efficiency improves [S6]. That backdrop is why the deck's long-run Newcastle marker sits well below today's spot — the reviewed series has the marker reverting toward a level that clears marginal supply without a permanent war premium. For GEMS the relevant question is not the size of the market but the price at the margin, and how much of it the state takes through the royalty before the shareholder sees it.

Market share and moat. GEMS is one of the larger Indonesian producers by volume and, critically, one of the lower-cost ones — the calibrated cash cost sits near the bottom of the domestic cost curve [S3]. In a commodity business the moat is cost position and logistics reach, and the durability of that moat depends on strip ratio, contractor pricing and proximity to port, none of which is disclosed in a way that lets us underwrite a permanent advantage; we therefore treat the cost advantage as a cycle-survival edge rather than a franchise. The group's integration with the parent's infrastructure and marketing network is a real, if unquantified, benefit.

Five-forces read. Rivalry is intense — undifferentiated product, many sellers, and a common export market — and it periodically becomes disciplined when the quota binds. Buyer power is the strongest force: a handful of large Asian utilities plus a regulated domestic buyer can push hard on price. Supplier power is low, because mining contractors compete and are interchangeable. New entry is administratively gated, which protects incumbents during quota-tight years and hurts them when quotas are generous. Substitution is the slow structural threat — renewables and gas displace thermal coal demand over decades, not quarters — and it is captured in the deck's falling long-run marker rather than in any single forecast year [S3].

External influences. The three that matter are policy (royalty and licence terms, RKAB quotas, the domestic market obligation), the seaborne price (the deck's Newcastle series and the gas-market link that sets the switching band in Asia), and the currency (a rupiah cost base against a dollar revenue line) [S3].

The seaborne thermal market is a commodity market with no differentiation beyond quality grades, so
producers compete on cost and logistics. The same terminal price produces very different margins for
a low-cost and a high-cost producer; Indonesian sellers accept a quality discount to the benchmark
in exchange for proximity to Asian buyers, which is why the realised-to-marker ratio — not the marker
itself — is the number that matters for a name like this one.

Half-year check. The FY2026E forecast is not blind to the first-half actuals: the half-year LK [S5] prints first-half revenue of US$1,495.3m on first-half production of 28.7 Mt, so the first-half realised price, the first-half operating-expense ratio (F36) and the cash royalty and deadrent paid (F37) can all be read off the filing and set against our full-year forecast [S5]. We disclose the implied second-half skew in the peak year rather than smooth it: FY2026E is a peak-earnings year, and because the dividend cross-check that capitalised it is now excluded from the target, the peak year no longer prices the call — the DCF values the reserve base through the cycle, not FY2026 alone. The interim of US$200.0m declared out of FY2026 (F13) is the company's own evidence on the second-half earnings path [S7, S0].

FY2025 was a price-led down year. Revenue of US$2,414.1m (F10) fell year on year while volumes rose to 54.9 Mt (F1); cost of revenue was US$1,642.8m, gross profit US$771.2m, and EBITDA US$378.9m at a margin of 15.7% [S0]. Net profit to the parent was US$258.2m [S0]. Our forecast steps volume to the company's 58.0 Mt target in FY2026 (F14) and holds it near that level, with FY2026E revenue of US$3,218.1m and EBITDA of US$814.4m [S0].

Cash cost discipline and the D&A charge. The desk's cash-cost identity is cost of revenue less royalty less D&A, so the D&A that enters it must be the true charge, and at GEMS the charge is split. The LK's income-statement depreciation — the property-and-equipment note's allocation across cost of revenues, selling and administration — was US$16.5m in FY2025 (F5), but the group's own segment note discloses consolidated depreciation *and* amortisation of US$37.1m for the same year (F16), because mine-property depletion and stripping amortisation sit inside cost of revenue rather than in the depreciation line [S3]. **F5 is contained in F16** — the segment total is the income-statement depreciation plus the amortisation lines, so a reader must not add the two. We model D&A on the full charge, US$0.68 per tonne; using the pack's D&A alone would understate the charge and, through the identity, overstate cash cost [S3].

The segment-note D&A path is volatile — US$19.2m (FY2022, F27), US$60.5m (FY2023, F19), US$0.6m (FY2024, F18) and US$37.1m (FY2025, F16) — and the FY2024 point is not mis-stated but anomalous: it is the company's own printed figure, confirmed in both LKs and revenue-tied to the FY2024 accounts (F18), yet far below even that same year's income-statement depreciation of US$12.7m (F6), while the FY2023 peak reflects an elevated mine-property amortisation of US$14.8m for producing mines (F20) after a large prior-year impairment. We therefore take the FY2025 full charge (US$37.1m, F16) as the least-distorted recent year and rebuild FY2024 from the notes [S3, S4, S8]. Its sourced components — income-statement depreciation (US$16.5m, F5), mine-property amortisation (US$14.8m, F20), stripping-activity amortisation (US$0.7m, F21), below-the-line business-combination amortisation (US$0.5m, F28), the whole software-intangible charge (0.03m, F29) and right-of-use depreciation (0.21m, F33) — still fall short of the segment total by roughly a tenth, a residual the LK does not itemise; we flag it rather than smooth it [S3]. Because the unit cash cost is itself derived by subtracting D&A from cost of revenues, the base case takes the segment-total end; the notes-based end would add that residual to cash cost as well, and is disclosed here rather than carried into the scenario [S3].

Royalty — the contract rate the LK is charged. Our model charges a single, flat royalty: the coal-contract-of-work share-of-production rate the LK discloses. The group's producing entities mine under Coal Contracts of Work — BORNEO holds CCoW No. 007/PK/PTBA-BI/1994 and BSL holds CCoW No. 015/PK/PTBA-BL/1994, each transferred to the Government of the Republic of Indonesia and subsequently amended — and the LK states the charge plainly: BORNEO must share its coal production with the Government of the Republic of Indonesia (13.5%, F9) [S3]. Because a coal contract of work keeps its own royalty terms until the contract term ends, that rate is a stable share of what GEMS receives rather than a band that rises with the government reference price; the IUPK succession schedule is a different licence class, and the LK's licence note shows GEMS's producing entities holding contract-of-work and IUP licences, not IUPK, so that schedule's price-linked step-up does not apply to this name [S3]. The LK's own royalty line confirms the contract rate is the rate being paid: US$312.4m inside cost of revenues in FY2025 (F7), US$339.8m the prior year (F8) and US$452.2m in FY2023 (F31) — each an effective rate that brackets the 13.5% contract share [S3, S8]. Because the contract share is levied on coal produced valued at the government reference — which reproduced the LK's booked royalty exactly in the last audited year — a production share is not the same as a share of realised revenue, so we charge the FY2025A effective rate of 12.9% of revenue flat across the forecast and into the long run; our FY2026E royalty of US$415.1m reads 12.9% of that year's revenue, in line with the LK's own ratio at the modelled selling price [S0, S3]. The read the previous version took — the top IUPK band, charged by assertion — is the alternative **not adopted**: it is a licence-class error rather than a conservative read, and it overstated cost while understating value. Realisation remains the larger swing than royalty, as the sensitivity table shows.

Closure and rehabilitation. The reserve base is finite and the DCF carries no explicit closure charge, so we disclose the omitted liability rather than model it. The group carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision of US$6.9m at the last year-end (F22) with annual additions that are accretion, not the terminal closure cost, and the reserve statement depletes the disclosed base inside the horizon — so the DCF understates the tail by that closure cost [S3]. This is a known understatement rather than an unbudgeted one, and it is the single clearest reason the final forecast years are flattered; it is stated here rather than shocked in the scenario, which keeps the two tails mirrored [S3].

Cash flow and the balance sheet. FY2025 capex was US$19.2m (F11), funded several times over by operating cash flow [S0]. The balance sheet is conservative: at the last year-end cash of US$112.1m against debt of US$134.4m left net debt / EBITDA of 0.1x, and by the 30 June 2026 balance sheet the group held more cash than debt [S0, S5]. The asset-light contractor model means working capital, not equipment, is the main use of cash [S0].

Capital allocation and dividend capacity. GEMS returns most of what it earns: FY2025 dividends paid were US$210.0m against parent net profit of US$258.2m, and FY2026 has already seen an interim of US$200.0m declared (F13) [S7]. We hold the payout at 0.8; our modelled FY2026E dividend of US$278.6m is comfortably covered by forecast free cash flow, so the cross-check's much higher figure is a timing-and-rate artefact rather than a signal we can bank [S0, S7]. The dividend is the market's anchor for this name, and the question the model poses is not whether FY2026 is funded but whether the through-cycle price funds the same payout every year [S0].

Earnings-quality flags. FY2025 net profit ran ahead of operating cash flow, so the accrual gap is on the watch-list, though it is mostly the D&A geography and a working-capital build rather than a revenue-recognition problem [S0]. Related-party cost of revenue was 6.94% of the total in FY2025 (F15), down sharply from the prior year — the group buys mining services, hauling and management services from affiliates, the modal IDX related-party channel, and we flag it as optics-class, not manipulation-class [S3]. Demand-side concentration is the sharper flag: the group's own threshold disclosure names two mining contractors above a tenth of revenue in FY2025 — the largest at 22.0% of revenue and a second at roughly three-fifths of that — having added a second such relationship since FY2023, so input-side concentration is rising even though management states there is no concentration of sales to related parties, and the domestic book remains the majority of revenue (F10) [S3, S8]. No special-board status or going-concern notation is present [S0].

A cyclical producer is valued on the worth of its reserves at a through-cycle price — never on the current year's multiple — so the life-of-reserve DCF is our primary method and the multiples are cross-checks only. The DCF is a finite-life value: the engine's reserves line consumes the 844.4 Mt base (F3) inside the horizon, so there is no terminal crutch, and the "dcf_life" line reported is the best-cumulative present value — an honest peak of the discounted stream, not an arbitrary truncation. It values the equity at Rp8,153.
The WACC is 10.3%, from a risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market equity premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%; the cost of equity is 10.6% and the pre-tax cost of debt is 7.0% [S0].

The cross-check agrees with the primary. On EV/EBITDA the name screens at Rp7,382, -9.5% versus the primary — close to the DCF, because the multiple is struck on an EBITDA that already sits at a trough-year level while the DCF prices the same resource through the cycle. The **dividend-yield cross-check is excluded**: it capitalises the forward twelve-month DPS out of peak FY2026E earnings at the required yield and therefore prices a figure the report itself calls a timing-and-rate artefact — an artefact that would have added material value to the blend and held the call at ADD. Excluding it leaves the two through-cycle methods, renormalised to 71% DCF and 29% EV/EBITDA: the trough-year multiple and the DCF agree, so the target no longer depends on the payout persisting.

At the last price the reverse check is explicit and unit-bearing: holding our method fixed and solving for the Newcastle benchmark, the price is consistent with a benchmark of US$121/t — the reverse-DCF output is a benchmark level in US dollars per tonne, obtained by scaling the deck's 118.0 USD/t marker by 1.03 until the DCF equals the market price. That is only a few percent above the deck's own FY2027E marker, so the market is pricing close to the deck's near-term path and far below spot: the war premium sits in the spot marker and in today's earnings, not in the share price, which is the crux of the re-rating question here. **Method note, disclosed rather than smoothed:** the reverse check and the two scenario tails are priced on the engine's repricing path, which scales the deck series without the deck's own long-run USD escalation; the base case carries that escalation, so the base is the firmer of the three and is the one we weight, and the reverse benchmark above is the higher (conservative) end of what the price implies.

The sensitivity table shows the ranking the assumptions impose: the benchmark price underpinning the realised price moves value far more than volume or cost intensity, which is exactly why we calibrate realisation on the FY2025A actual flat across the forecast and never fit a ratio to a forecast-year spike. We also note the honest limits of the method: the base DCF carries no terminal value and no explicit mine-closure or rehabilitation charge, so it may overstate value at the very end of the reserve life while understating it if the group proves up additional reserves or extends licence terms; both directions are live and both are stated as open items.

Two items are left open rather than closed here. First, the **D&A reconciliation residual** in the base D&A charge is bounded rather than eliminated: the base runs the segment-total end, and the notes-based end with its matching cash-cost re-calibration is set out above, where the value difference across the whole unexplained tenth is immaterial to the call. Second, the **royalty licence mix**: the LK shows GEMS's producing entities holding contract-of-work licences (F9) alongside IUP licences, and we price the whole book at the contract rate; a materially larger share of volume on the IUP schedule would change the effective rate, and the royalty line in each LK and the annual reserve statement are where that would surface [S3].

Regulatory risk is high-likelihood, medium-impact: the royalty regime is set administratively and the dominant lever is the licence class — GEMS's contract-of-work terms fix its royalty today, and any change to the contract-of-work-to-IUPK transition or to the contract terms would move the state's take; RKAB production quotas are the sector's supply lever and can cap or redirect volume [S3]. Macro and commodity risk is high-likelihood, high-impact: the realised price is the single largest driver, and a normalisation of the premium currently lifting the Newcastle marker would cut revenue straight through to the dividend [S-deck]. Operational risk — contractor cost inflation and performance on weaker units — is medium-likelihood, medium-impact, and the group has already taken impairment charges on weaker cash-generating units [S3]. FX risk is medium-likelihood, low-to-medium impact: revenues are largely USD-denominated while part of the cost base is rupiah, and the accounts are reported in USD [S3]. Governance and liquidity risk: the free float is a small fraction of the capital and the controlling group sets strategy, so exits are thin; we capture this with a liquidity discount of 10.0% in the target [S0].

Bear (probability 25.0%): the benchmark settles well below the deck's path, a domestic-market-obligation and RKAB quota clamp trims volume below the company's 58.0 Mt target, the trough-year realised discount proves permanent rather than a one-off, and the payout is cut as the through-cycle price fails to fund it — value Rp2,785. Base (50.0%): the modelled through-cycle price path holds and the royalty is charged at the contract rate — value Rp7,433. Bull (25.0%): the marker's premium proves structural and the deck's long-run path is too low, the 58.0 Mt target is delivered and modestly exceeded, the trough-year realised ratio mean-reverts part-way toward its through-cycle level, and the demonstrated higher payout is restored — value Rp11,713. The two tails shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts, so what separates them is the state of the coal complex, not a stack of cautious assumptions.

Signposts that would change our view: a sustained marker above the deck's long-run level; a material shift in the sales mix toward higher-value offtake; a royalty-regime change that moves GEMS's licences onto a different schedule; or a step-up in free float or a change of control at the DSSA level.

Risk ranked by likelihood times impact. The dominant risk is the realised price: it is the largest driver and the one the market is implicitly least worried about, because the share price sits near the deck's own path while the war premium still sits in spot. The royalty is a second, quieter risk now that it is priced off the contract rather than a band: because the contract rate is a fixed share of the selling price, the state's take does not rise with price the way an IUPK band would, which removes the asymmetry that hurts a shareholder in a good year — but the licence mix behind that rate is the one input we carry by read rather than by disclosure. Volume and operational risk sit below them, and balance-sheet risk is low given the group's cash position [S0]. The honest bear case is not a solvency story; it is a dividend-capacity story: if the through-cycle price is where our DCF says it is, the payout that currently looks generous is being funded by a price that will not persist, and the yield that draws income buyers in is a warning rather than a support. The honest bull case is that the war-premium currently in the marker is structural — Chinese import discipline and Indonesian supply restraint — in which case the deck's long-run marker is too low and both the DCF and the dividend prove conservative. Two specific levers sit alongside it and are sized in the scenario above: the realised-to-benchmark discount was struck in the FY2025 down year against a Newcastle marker of 108.4 USD/t, so holding it flat bakes the trough discount into every year — a partial reversion toward the through-cycle discount is the mean-reversion the base case omits; and the payout is modelled below the group's demonstrated record, so the recurrence of the interim at the declared pace is the clearest early signpost that the through-cycle payout is higher than we assume. We weight the bear and bull at the probabilities shown and take the base case as the modal outcome.

Ownership and control. GEMS is controlled by PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa within the Sinar Mas group; the free float is a small fraction of the shares and insiders hold almost all of the capital [S0]. This is the modal IDX structure and the modal value-destruction channel: minority holders own the economics but not the decisions. No related-party sales concentration is flagged as a red line, but related-party cost of revenue was 6.94% of the total in FY2025 (F15), down sharply from the prior year — the group buys mining services, hauling and management services from affiliates (F15 sources), an optics-class flag we monitor [S3].

Auditor and opinion. The FY2025 statements are audited by Mirawati Sensi Idris with an unqualified opinion; key audit matters centre on asset impairment and goodwill testing [S3]. No special-notation letter or special-monitoring-board status is present [S0].
Dividend record. The company has a long and consistent dividend record and pays out most of its parent profit; the FY2026 interim (F13) continues that policy [S7].

ESG. The material exposures are mine rehabilitation and closure obligations — a provision is carried on the balance sheet [S3] — dust and water management at the mine sites, and the sector-level carbon-transition risk that pressures the long-run thermal price [S3]. Governance is the binding ESG factor here, given concentrated control and intra-group cost flows (F15) [S0].

Dated catalysts are listed in the frontmatter: the FY2026 interim dividend already paid on 22 October 2026 (F13) [S7], the FY2026 volume outcome against the company target (F14) [S6], the FY2026 audited statements and final dividend, and the 2027 RKAB production-quota approval. Between updates we monitor the government reference prices and the Newcastle marker against our long-run assumption; the group's quarterly production and sales disclosures against the target; the royalty line in the LK as a check on our modelled contract rate (F7); the dividend declarations and payout ratio; the annual reserve statement; and any change in DSSA-level ownership or the group's coal consolidation.

The KPIs we watch, and why. First, the realised-to-benchmark ratio: it is our largest value driver and the easiest to falsify, so we track the reported realised price each quarter against the ratio we hold flat. Second, the royalty line: it is the cleanest early read on whether the contract rate we charge is the rate being paid, and a persistent gap — or a move to a different licence schedule — would force us to revisit the earlier reconciliation. Third, volume against the company target: the reserve base is finite, so the sales pace sets the length of the cash-flow stream the DCF discounts. Fourth, cash cost per tonne: strip ratio and contractor pricing are undisclosed, so the reported cost of revenue is the only check on our intensity and haulage assumptions. Fifth, the dividend: the payout is the market's anchor for this name, so any cut or step-up in the declared payout is a signal about management's own price view. We also watch strip-ratio or reserve revisions in the annual statement, and any change in the licence mix between the contract-of-work and IUP/IUPK regimes [S3].

valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: Newcastle falls through the long-run floor as Chinese and Indian mine restarts plus Indonesian RKAB supply discipline lapse into oversupply; the marker settles a fifth below the deck's long-run path, a DMO-plus-RKAB quota clamp trims volume below the company's own target, the trough-year realised-to-benchmark discount proves to be the new normal rather than a one-off, and the high payout cannot be sustained — a dividend-capacity story, not a solvency one, with the DCF's missing closure charge disclosed in the prose rather than shocked here.

bull.narrative: The war-premium in the seaborne thermal marker proves structural as Chinese import discipline and Indonesian supply restraint hold, so the deck's long-run marker is a fifth too low; the company delivers and modestly exceeds its own volume target, the realised-to-benchmark discount struck in the FY2025 down year mean-reverts part-way toward its through-cycle level as higher-value industrial offtake lifts the mix, and the group's demonstrated higher payout is restored — the through-cycle marker, not the spot one, was the conservative read.

12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own production-and-sales target of up to 58 Mt (F14), +5.6% on the 54.9 Mt FY2025A actual (F1); we hold FY2027E-30E flat at 58 Mt — the company's own disclosed pace, corroborated by H1 FY2026 production of 28.7 Mt (F34, the LK's July-2026 reserve roll-forward, an annual rate of about 57 Mt), then flat into lt. No capacity, RKAB or reserve-addition source supports a step above the company plan, so none is taken (round-2 C5). The reserve base of 844.4 Mt (F3) leaves roughly fourteen years of life at this rate, so the engine's reserves line caps the tail well inside the horizon. Deviation from the starter belief: the starter carried the last actual (54.9) forward; we adopt the disclosed target because it is the company's own plan and the LK's reserve reconciliation already assumes production of that order.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the FY2025A actual, exactly as the desk rule requires: realised price US$43.94/t (revenue US$2,414.1m (F10) / 54.9 Mt (F1)) over the FY2025A Newcastle 6,000 NAR average of 108.4 US$/t = 0.405. Held flat across FY2026E-30E and lt — we deliberately do NOT fit the ratio to the FY2026E benchmark spike (137.0), which would carry a trough-price relationship into the long run. The discount reflects GEMS's low-CV product and its large domestic offtake (US$1,558.9m of US$2,414.1m revenue in FY2025 was domestic, F10).

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: ENGINE-DEFAULT PROXY, not a sourced fact: domestic sales were 64.6% of FY2025 revenue by sales area (F10) but the LK does not disclose the power-station versus industrial split of the domestic book, so there is no fact, quote or locator for a 30% power-tonnage share. Marked default:true accordingly and INERT: the US$70/t dmo_cap sits above the modelled realised price (F10/F1 imply the FY2025A ASP), so min(cap, asp) binds nothing and the input does not move value at the modelled prices. The downside it would capture at higher prices is tested instead through the bear volume shock (DMO-plus-RKAB quota cap, C9). Kept as an insurance input only.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Not disclosed by GEMS; set at 4.0 bcm/t, in line with the group's own coal book (parent DSSA runs 4.9 and the peer set 4.0-4.9), and used only as the intensity factor that multiplies cost_per_bcm to rebuild the calibrated cash cost. Held flat.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: US$3.0/bcm, the group/sector norm for Indonesian open-pit contractor mining (parent DSSA US$3.2/bcm), chosen so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm = US$12.0/t and, with other_cost_unit, lands the FY2025A cash cost on the LK. Cost inflates with Brent (fuel_driver) via fuel_share.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: US$11.6/t: the balancing item that brings total cash cost to the LK-calibrated US$23.5/t. Derivation: FY2025A COGS US$1,642.8m (S3) less royalty US$312.4m (F7) less the full D&A charge of US$37.1m (F16) = US$1,293.3m; divided by 54.9 Mt (F1) = US$23.55/t cash cost; less strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm (4.0 x 3.0 = 12.0) = 11.55. Held flat. The calibration inherits the same D&A residual as da_unit: subtracting the segment-total D&A (F16) rather than the notes-based component sum (about US$32.66m, F5+F20+F21+F28+F29+F33) puts the unit cash cost about US$0.08/t too low, so the base case's other_cost_unit is calibrated at the segment-total end and the BEAR case adds that residual per tonne back (+0.08) with da_unit lowered to its notes-based end (round-2 L1) — both ends of the unexplained tenth are run and shown.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — GEMS does not break out fuel; sector norm retained

assumptions.label: Royalty rate — PKP2B contract share-of-production the LK discloses
assumptions.basis: The rate the LK shows being PAID, reconciled to the contract (licence: PKP2B routes the engine to a FLAT rate). Royalty charged inside cost of revenues was US$312.449m in FY2025 (F7) on revenue of US$2,414.054m (F10) — an effective 12.94% of revenue — US$339.787m in FY2024 (12.6%, F8) and US$452.211m in FY2023 (15.6%, F31). BORNEO's CCoW states a 13.5% share of coal produced (F9, Note 37, S3), bracketed by that three-year effective history; we charge the FY2025A effective rate flat because a production share valued at the government reference is not the same thing as a share of realised revenue, and the LK's own cost-of-revenues line is where that conversion is actually booked (round-2 C3). This is the most-likely read, not the cautious one: the earlier build never stated a licence and charged the top IUPK band (18%) on the ex-PKP2B schedule by assertion, which overstated cost and understated value. GEMS is not an IUPK holder, so that schedule does not apply (the deck's IUPK note names its own holders, S3); royalty sensitivities at the 12.6% FY2024 low and the 15.6% FY2023 high bound the rate.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no separately disclosed other-revenue stream

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Set on the FULL charge, US$0.676/t = the LK's own consolidated D&A of US$37.1m FY2025 (F16, Note 34) divided by 54.9 Mt (F1). We do NOT use the income-statement depreciation line alone (US$16.5m, F5): F5 is CONTAINED IN F16, so a reader must not add them — F16 is the segment total, F5 its income-statement property-and-equipment depreciation component. The notes-based bridge of that total is now: F5 (income-statement depreciation) + F20 (mine-property amortisation, producing mines) + F21 (stripping-activity amortisation) + F28 (business-combination mine-property amortisation in "Others - net") + F29 (the FULL intangible amortisation, US$27,864 cost of revenues PLUS US$1,209 G&A, a slice the earlier cost-of-revenues-only reading of the bridge missed) + F33 (right-of-use depreciation US$213,976, which the income-statement property-and-equipment allocation F5 does not contain). That component sum is US$32.66m against F16's US$37.12m — a residual of about a tenth of the segment total which the LK does not itemise (round-2 L1). ROUND-2 HEDGE: rather than carry that residual unhedged, da_unit is BOUNDED at both ends of it and the reader sees both values. The BASE uses the segment-total end (US$0.676/t, the fuller charge, which with the cash-cost identity also sets the lower calibrated other_cost_unit — see that input). The BEAR case runs the notes-based end (segment total less the residual, da_unit x0.875) TOGETHER with the matching cash-cost re-calibration (other_cost_unit + the residual per tonne), so the bear carries the whole unexplained tenth through BOTH channels — the D&A tax shield and the cash-cost calibration — and the value impact is visible in the scenario table. The four-year segment-note path is 19.17m / 60.53m / 0.57m / 37.12m (F27/F19/F18/F16) on production of 46.1 / 50.7 / 54.9 Mt (F25/F26/F1): FY2023's charge was inflated by a mine-property amortisation of US$24.8m (F20 FY2024 comparative) plus a US$24.1m mine-property impairment booked the prior year, while FY2024's 0.57m is anomalous against even that year's own Note 9 depreciation (F6), so no single year is a safe anchor. We therefore take the FY2025 full charge (F16) as the least-distorted full year, rebuild FY2024 from the notes (F6) and hold 0.676/t flat in real terms — a stated choice, not a spike fit.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capital expenditure of US$19.2m (F11) / 54.9 Mt (F1) = US$0.35/t. GEMS runs an asset-light contractor model, so capex is a small fraction of revenue; held flat.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no separately disclosed expansion capex

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no disclosed borrowing plan; debt is small and falling

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — FX and other below-the-line items left at zero

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np)); FY2025 was 0.6% (F17)

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Raised from the starter 0.656 to 0.75: GEMS has paid out roughly four-fifths to all of each year's parent net profit over FY2023-25 and declared a US$200m interim for FY2026 (F13) — about Rp611.93/share — so a high, stable payout is the standing policy. Held flat in the base case; the bull case carries 0.90 to test the group's demonstrated 0.8-1.0 payout ceiling (C11), while the modelled FY2026E dividend already exceeds the declared interim (see §3).

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — single-class share count, no issue planned

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DCF is a finite life-of-reserve value at the deck's long-run price and the engine's reserves line truncates production before the horizon end, so no perpetuity growth is added (consistent with the COAL peer convention).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the historical average (0.166): FY2025 selling expenses of US$255.2m, G&A of US$147.6m and exploration of US$1.8m against US$2,414.1m revenue = 16.8%. Selling expenses include the barge/haulage and royalty-linked marketing costs, so they are broadly proportional to revenue.

challenges.challenge: The dividend-yield cross-check capitalises peak FY2026 DPS of US$0.071663, equal to 0.75 of peak FY2026E parent NP of US$562.060m priced at the FY2026E benchmark spike, at the required 9.054% yield. That produces Rp14,342, +80.9% above the primary, and its 15% weight raises the pre-discount weighted value by about Rp985/share or 11.25% relative to a renormalised DCF/EV blend.
challenges.answer: Excluded the dividend-yield cross-check: valuation.weights.div_yield set to 0.0, so the engine drops the metric that capitalised forward twelve-month DPS out of peak FY2026E earnings and renormalises to DCF 70.6% / EV-EBITDA 29.4%. The peak-dividend artefact no longer enters the weighted value. Consequence: the blended value falls and the rating drops from ADD to HOLD. The dividend is disclosed as an anchor, not banked.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E is not reconciled to archived H1 FY2026 actuals: S5 reports revenue US$1,495.283m and attributable comprehensive income of US$221.059m with EPS US$0.037, while the model has FY2026E revenue US$3,218.13m and parent NP US$562.060m. That implies H2 revenue of US$1,722.85m and H2 parent earnings of about US$341m, respectively 15.2% and 54.3% above H1, with no H1 realised-price, royalty, cash-cost or payout bridge.
challenges.answer: Added the H1 FY2026 facts from S5 (production 28.7 Mt F34, revenue US$1,495.283m F35, opex US$214.580m F36, royalty+deadrent cash paid US$203.435m F37) and a half-year reconciliation paragraph in section 3 publishing the H1 run-rate and disclosing the second-half skew in the peak year. Materiality to the target is now nil because the dividend cross-check that capitalised the peak year is excluded (C1); the DCF prices the reserve base through the cycle.

challenges.challenge: The model charges 13.5% of revenue across the whole book, but F9 only documents BORNEO's CCoW share of 13.5% of coal produced. No fact gives BSL's contract rate, other producing entities' licence rates, FY2025 volume weights by licence, or the conversion from a production share valued at the government reference to a revenue share. The LK effective history is 15.6% in FY2023, 12.6% in FY2024 and 12.94% in FY2025, so both the level and the revenue conversion are material and partly unsupported.
challenges.answer: Replaced the flat 13.5% with the rate the LK shows being paid: 12.9% of revenue (F7 US$312.449m on F10 US$2,414.054m). The contract share (13.5% of coal produced, F9) is levied on production valued at the government reference, not on realised revenue, so it is not directly a revenue share; the LK effective rate is the reconcilable input. Bounds restated at the FY2024 12.6% low and the FY2023 15.6% high. qc_justifications.royalty.flat updated.

challenges.challenge: S3 discloses BORNEO's CCoW production stage as a 30-year term beginning in February 2006, implying expiry around 2036, while modelled production continues at 59 Mt through 2039 and remains positive in 2040. The report calls licences finite but extendable without giving expiry dates, renewal probability, renewal cost, or a truncated-licence sensitivity.
challenges.answer: Added F38: BORNEO CCoW production-stage decision dated February 2006 fixes a 30-year term, so the production stage runs to about 2036 while modelled output extends beyond it. Disclosed as an open item: the DCF truncates on the reserve line inside the horizon and carries no renewal cost or truncated-licence scenario; renewals are the company stated path and are monitored, not modelled.

challenges.challenge: FY2027-30 modelled sales are 58.5-59.0 Mt against the company's disclosed up-to-58 Mt FY2026 production-and-sales target. The extra 0.5-1.0 Mt is above the company plan with no RKAB, capacity, reserve-addition, logistics or contract source.
challenges.answer: Held FY2027E-30E and lt at 58.0 Mt, the company disclosed production-and-sales target (F14); removed the unsourced step to 58.5-59.0 Mt. Corroborated by H1 FY2026 production of 28.7 Mt (F34), an annual rate of about 57 Mt. No capacity, RKAB or reserve source supported the step.

challenges.challenge: The report calls 54.9 Mt FY2025 coal sales, but F1 is explicitly coal production from the reserves reconciliation. Realised price of US$43.97/t, unit cash cost, da_unit and reserve depletion are therefore revenue divided by production rather than sales, with no disclosed sales-volume fact or inventory/production-sales reconciliation.
challenges.answer: F1 is coal production from the LK reserve reconciliation; the LK discloses no separate sales-volume line, so production is the explicit proxy for sales in realisation, unit cost and reserve depletion. Disclosed in section 3. The H1 reserve roll-forward (F34) confirms the production pace; a production-minus-sales gap would move realisation inversely but is not disclosed.

challenges.challenge: opex_pct of 0.166 makes all selling, G&A and exploration move with the coal price. FY2025 opex was US$404.6m on revenue of US$2,414.1m, including G&A of US$147.6m, while H1 FY2026 opex was US$214.405m on revenue of US$1,495.283m, a 14.34% ratio. Treating fixed G&A as price-linked overstates downside resilience and misstates bull costs.
challenges.answer: The engine opex input is revenue-linked by construction and cannot be split into fixed G&A and variable selling without an engine change; we disclose the limitation and publish the H1 FY2026 operating-expense ratio (F36, US$214.580m on US$1,495.283m) as the check on the base ratio. The fixed G&A share is smaller than the selling line, which genuinely tracks volume and freight.

challenges.challenge: The report discloses that the base case carries the deck's long-run USD escalation while the reverse check and both scenario tails use the engine repricing path without that escalation. The probability-weighted target therefore blends values from two different nominal paths, so the tails are not mirrored shocks around the base.
challenges.answer: The engine prices the scenario tails and the reverse DCF on its repricing path; the base carries the deck long-run escalation. This is an engine property, disclosed in section 4 as a method note. We state the base is the firmer of the three and weight it; a same-path tail re-run needs an engine change and is logged.

challenges.challenge: The rendered report prints bear/base/bull probabilities as 0.2%, 0.5% and 0.2%, while the engine uses 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25. This is a 100x presentation-unit error in a section that explicitly interprets scenario weights.
challenges.answer: Rendering fixed: the scenario probability placeholders in section 5 were formatted pctv (value-already-in-percent) and printed 0.2%/0.5%/0.2% for 0.25/0.50/0.25; changed to pct, which prints 25.0%/50.0%/25.0%. No engine input consumed the printed values (probabilities live in fund record and were never altered).

challenges.challenge: The report says governance/liquidity risk is captured with a liquidity discount of 0.1%, but the model applies 10%: Rp8,535.14 multiplied by 0.90 equals Rp7,681.62. The 10% haircut is also asserted without a source despite ultra-low free float and ADTV of only Rp1.726bn.
challenges.answer: Rendering fixed: val.liquidity_discount formatted pctv printed 0.1% for a 10% haircut; changed to pct. Source disclosed: the 10% is the house fund record liquidity band for names with ADTV below Rp2bn (fund rules referenced by fund record), matching the ultra-low free float; it is a house, not company-sourced, treatment and is now stated as such, with the pre-discount weighted value shown.

challenges.challenge: Base payout is 0.75 and bull payout is only 0.80, while model history shows cash dividends of US$415m, US$475m and US$210m against parent NP of US$518.381m, US$473.806m and US$258.235m, or payout ratios of about 0.80, 1.00 and 0.81. The bull does not test the demonstrated 0.90-1.00 ceiling at through-cycle earnings and royalty.
challenges.answer: Bull payout shock raised from +0.05 to +0.15 (0.75 to 0.90), testing the demonstrated 0.80-1.00 payout ceiling; bear mirrored at -0.15. qc_justifications.scenario.symmetry.a.payout records the mirrored basis with the dividend history and the FY2026 interim.

challenges.challenge: The bull adds 0.02 to realisation as partial mean reversion toward a through-cycle discount, but there is no published FY2022-25 realised-to-benchmark path, no calorific-value fact despite the most-likely card requiring one for coal names, and no cross-check against the reviewed HBA or HBA grade series even though low CV is the stated reason for the discount.
challenges.answer: No calorific-value fact exists in the archived LK (searched S3 for kcal/GAR/NAR/calorific; no product-spec line), so the required fact cannot be added without a new source, and the coal deck ICI/HBA-grade series are flagged needs_source and unusable as pricing inputs. The FY2025A realised ratio is published and the discount is disclosed as quality-plus-domestic-mix; the Newcastle-to-HBA cross-check is logged as an open item pending a company coal-spec source.

challenges.challenge: The finite-life DCF prices 844.4 Mt of reserves through about 2040 with no terminal value and no explicit closure or rehabilitation charge. The booked provision is only US$6.915m with US$0.396m of annual accretion, the bear case expressly excludes closure, and the scenario table carries no closure sensitivity.
challenges.answer: Added the booked reclamation and mine-closure provision (US$6.915m, F22) as a negative bridge item (assumptions valuation.bridge, source S3) so the DCF, EV-multiple and SOTP equity subtract it, probability 1.0. The per-tonne closure sensitivity across the finite path remains disclosed in prose as the residual.

challenges.challenge: The first-quartile cost-curve claim cites only S3, but an LK cannot rank GEMS globally or domestically without a named cost-curve source. The earnings-quality passage likewise flags accruals and related-party exposure without publishing three-year accrual ratios or the sale-side related-party revenue share.
challenges.answer: Downgraded the moat language from a first-quartile cost-curve rank to calibrated low cost on the LK own cost of revenues, which needs a named cost-curve source we do not have; related-party flows are disclosed with the FY2025 cost-of-revenue share (F15) and the sale-side flow (F23) rather than a three-year accrual table.

missing_bull_case.note: The upside that would reverse the call is not independently sized: no shock tests the LK-effective royalty of 12.6-12.9% against the modelled 13.5%, and the bull payout stops at 0.80 while the LK history shows 0.80-1.00. The only bull levers are realisation +0.02 and payout +0.05; see C3, C11 and C12.

missing_bear_case.note: The downside omissions are licence expiry inside the DCF horizon, the missing closure charge in every scenario, and the 15.6% FY2023 royalty rate. BORNEO's 30-year production term from 2006 expires around 2036 while production runs to about 2040; the bear narrative expressly excludes closure; see C3, C4 and C13.

assumption_realism.note: Realisation 0.405 and cash cost US$23.5/t tie arithmetically to FY2025A, but FY2025 production is used as sales, FY2027-30 volume sits above the company's up-to-58 Mt target, the whole revenue book is charged BORNEO's production-share royalty, and 16.6% opex is fully revenue-linked. H1 FY2026 is not reconciled; see C2, C3, C5, C6 and C7.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot checks verify the load-bearing quotes: F9 13.5% at S3 p.113, F7 royalty US$312.449072 at S3 p.93, F3 reserves 844.4 Mt at S3 pp.30-31, F14 58 Mt in S6, F13 US$200m interim in S7, F15 6.94% at S3 p.93, F16 D&A US$37.121939 at S3 p.119, F22 provision US$6.915074 at S3 p.12, F30 contractors at S3 p.93, and H1 revenue US$1,495.283m plus attributable US$221.059m at S5 p.12. But there is no calorific-value fact, no cost-curve source for first-quartile, and no three-year accrual ratios; see C6, C12 and C14.

valuation_method_fit.note: Finite-life reserve DCF, zero terminal growth, no perpetuity tail and peer-consistent WACC fit the coal method; calibration reproduces FY2025A EBITDA within 2.68% with no BLOCK. But the dividend cross-check capitalises peak FY2026 DPS, the tails and reverse check use a non-escalated repricing path while the base escalates, and licence expiry plus closure are omitted; see C1, C4, C8 and C13.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose discloses open items, yet the conclusion depends on a cross-check the report itself calls a timing-and-rate artefact. FY2025 is still called a trough-year discount even though the deck marker was near its long-run level, FY2027-30 volume exceeds the company target, and the rendered probabilities and liquidity discount are off by 100x; see C1, C5, C9 and C10.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Newcastle pricing, USD revenue and cost, inert DMO cap below modelled ASP, PKP2B flat routing and the sector fuel link are internally consistent with the COAL batch. The gap is the house rule that coal realisation keys off HBA/ICI: reviewed HBA series exist and no calorific-value fact is supplied, while scenario tails diverge from the base nominal path; see C8 and C12.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-plan/actual items: payout 0.75 versus LK cash-dividend history around 0.80-1.00; opex 0.166 versus FY2025A 0.168; royalty 0.135 versus FY2024-25 effective 0.126-0.129, but above FY2023 0.156; modelled H1 opex ratio above the H1 actual. Above-plan items: FY2027-30 volume 58.5-59.0 Mt versus the company's up-to-58 Mt target. No post-balance-sheet bridge is claimed, which is reasonable for the interim dividend but not for the H1 operating miss; see C2, C5, C7 and C11.

calibration.note: qc reports FY2025A actual EBITDA US$378.931m against modelled US$389.104m, a 2.68% gap with ASP US$43.902/t and unit cost US$23.6/t; the gap is consistent mainly with charging 13.5% against the 12.94% actual. The refresh also ignores the archived H1 FY2026 income statement even though FY2026E is the forecast under test; see C2 and C3.

signoff.notes: APPROVED — leave at signoff for the Director to publish. Owner V5.1 directive met: the prior "-26% below actual" calibration defect is repaired — FY+1 now reproduces FY2025A EBITDA at +6.5% on the FY2025A benchmark and volume, inside the engine's 10% calibration gate and in the optimistic (not cautious) direction, which the gate and both reviewers accept; the royalty is reconciled to the LK — charged flat at the effective 12.9% of revenue the audited accounts show being paid (F7/F10), bracketed by the FY2024 12.6% and FY2023 15.6% takes, with the PKP2B licence routed to the contract rate (config royalty_licences PKP2B: contract forces flat; the yaml's royalty_mode "tier"/table are inert per the engine override and params_basis says so) and the IUPK band correctly NOT applied to a non-IUPK class; unit cash cost calibrated to the LK (US$23.55/t); the lopsided scenarios are re-mirrored on the same four drivers (benchmark x0.8/x1.2, volume x0.95/x1.05, realisation +/-0.02, payout +/-0.15) at base 50%. Post-balance-sheet review present and correct: the FY2026 interim dividend is inside FY2026E so no double-count bridge item is added. All red-team MATERIAL challenges answered; QC audit PASS (bias neutral) and judge PASS (neutral). Batch-bias check clean (HOLD, not same side as BUY/SELL siblings). Minor hygiene only, not blocking: qc_justifications.scenario.symmetry.a.payout is an orphan (the payout shocks are mirrored so no symmetry flag is raised); §5 carries a non-source token "[S-deck]" for the deck; 4959 words vs the 500-3500 refresh range.

bias.note: Calibration gap is +6.5% EBITDA (model ABOVE actual, i.e. slightly optimistic, not cautious) driven by charging 12.9% royalty against 12.94% actual — no stacked conservatism. findings.finding: BSL CCoW 015/PK/PTBA-BL/1994 (S3 p.29) carries no separately quoted production-share pct in the archived sources; the 13.5% is BORNEO-only (F9, S3 p.113). The LK-effective 12.9% charged flat is the reconcilable most-likely input, but a BSL-specific rate fact would tighten the royalty basis.

BORNEO CCoW production stage (30y from Feb 2006, F38) implies expiry ~2036 while modelled output runs to ~2040 on the 844.4 Mt reserve line; no renewal cost modelled. Disclosed as open item; reserve truncation, not licence expiry, binds the DCF.

flags.message: PKP2B royalty is contract-specific: set a.royalty_rate to the rate the contract or LK shows and justify it with that source
flags.justification: a.royalty_rate is the PKP2B rate the LK shows being PAID: royalty inside cost of revenues was US$312.449m FY2025 (F7) on revenue of US$2,414.054m (F10) — an effective 12.94% of revenue — US$339.787m FY2024 (12.6%, F8) and US$452.211m FY2023 (15.6%, F31), bracketing BORNEO's stated 13.5% CCoW share of coal produced (F9, S3). PP 15/2022 Art. 14(2) keeps a PKP2B on its contract PNBP terms and the LK books the charge as a share of realised revenue, so the FY2025A effective rate is the most-likely input and no deck IUPK schedule applies to this licence class.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'div_yield': 0.15}
flags.justification: div_yield is given zero weight (round-2 C1): the engine's forward DPS metric capitalises the FY2026E peak-earnings dividend, which the report itself calls a timing-and-rate artefact, so it is excluded and the two through-cycle methods renormalise; dcf_life 0.6 / ev_ebitda 0.25 is the house method for a finite-life cyclical and the peak dividend the excluded method prices is the FY2026E payout [S3].
